utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, General. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I believe we have already worked in the same composition, and I gather that the appearances are the same. Good afternoon to the counsel of the Prosecution; good afternoon, counsel for Defence. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The case number IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is representing the Prosecution today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours. We are representing the Prosecution in the following composition: Mr. Michael Blaxill, Ms. Sureta Chana, and myself, Franck Terrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could the Defence counsel please introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Attorney Nikola Kostic appearing with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Pursuant to the scheduling order of the 4th of July, 2000, we are going to have a Status Conference which will be followed by a motion hearing on the motion for provisional release submitted by General Galic. That is why Judge Riad and Judge Wald are present here with myself, who is acting as a Pre-Trial Judge on this Status Conference. We will proceed with the Status Conference first. The scheduling order contains the agenda for the present Status Conference, and the first point to be discussed today is the disclosure of materials pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and Rule 68. Could the Prosecutor now tell us how we stand on this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Michael Blaxill will inform you on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Michael Blaxill, you have the floor. Let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon. Indeed, the first two items of your agenda are items which I am specifically assigned to address. In the first case, the disclosure of materials in respect of Rule 66(A)(ii), the disclosure to date has been two substantial shipments encompassing virtually all the witness statements in the possession of the Prosecutor, a list of witnesses -- I say a list, a number of witnesses which essentially goes beyond those even that we hope or propose to call in the final analysis. However, we have endeavoured to discover as widely as possible. That has included, where we have possessed -- have them in our possession, prior statements by any of those witnesses, and at this time excludes, I think, only certain witnesses where the provisions of Rule 70 currently apply and in respect of which we are seeking the appropriate release. That is anticipated to be obtained in the not too distance future, but I cannot put a firm or fixed date on it, but a matter of a very few weeks, I think, to clear that issue. I think that relates to probably no more than four or five statements we currently hold and would propose disclosing. As regards the compliance at this stage, therefore, with witness statements, we hope we have substantially complied, but there has been one logistical problem, and that is that on the last occasion, two boxes of disclosure, including some of those statements I've referred to, they were sent on the 9th of June this year by a firm called OPL Courier Service. Regrettably, of those two boxes dispatched on the 9th of June, one box was received by Mr. Kostic on the 12th, and we understand the other has gone missing. A proper check has been undertaken, and, in fact, we have a report dated this day indicating that so far, that box is deemed to have gone astray. In order not to delay matters further, as it is nearly a month now that this thing has gone astray, we can, I understand, recreate the contents of that box and redispatch within the next seven day, seven working days. So that is, in so sense, a novus actus interveniens. We couldn't anticipate such a loss. We can endeavour to remedy it within, as I say, the next week to week and a half, including delivery time. With regard to compliance with Rule 68, that has run essentially hand and glove, and any materials that we do so identify will be disclosed to the Defence; and we will do so on the basis of the fact that this is, of course, an ongoing obligation of the Prosecution and which will basically not come to an end throughout the proceedings, so that at any given time, we will obviously have endeavoured to serve all and any Rule 68 material. But one can never be certain that further investigations, even in other cases, may produce something which, as I say, would be served in accordance with the ongoing obligation. That is all I would propose to mention to Your Honours at this stage in relation to item 1. Unless you have any specific question on that, I could, with your leave, move to item number 2 and the other pre-trial preparations and filings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blaxill, I prefer that we deal with each issue in turn, and let us give the Defence the opportunity to respond. I don't know whether Mr. Kostic has any comments to make in response to what the Prosecutor has just stated. It is quite regrettable that a box of documents would have gone missing. Mr. Kostic indicated that he would prefer that the documents be sent by mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Blaxill is correct. We did receive one shipment and did not receive the other shipment, and we are trying from our side to trace the documents. There is a procedure that's used. Whether we'll be successful on our end, I don't know. We will try. I have not received any documents which have specifically been identified as Rule 68 disclosures. I'm assuming that if such documents exist and the Prosecution feels that they are exculpatory in nature, that they might earmark them, and that would certainly be helpful. So that is as much as I can tell you, Your Honour, at this point, on number 1 of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let us move on to item number 2, progress towards completing -- actually, progress in agreeing on undisputed matters of law and fact pursuant to Rule 65 ter, (E)(ii) and (iii). I am aware of the quantity of the documents which have already been disclosed to the Defence and that the Defence has to analyse. However, I hope that both parties have begun their co-operation amongst themselves since the last Status Conference. If you remember, I suggested that a meeting should take place between the two parties before the Prosecutor goes to the United States. I should like to know at this point whether the parties have had a chance to meet in the meantime. Mr. Blaxill, could you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, we have not had an opportunity to spend any meaningful length of time with Mr. Kostic. That is clearly just -- it seems a logistics problem at this time. He was able to meet with us fairly briefly, and we discussed the question after the last Status Conference, and indeed we submitted initially a -- let us say a taster of a set of facts, at least, that we might ask him to consider so that we would get some flavour of how we would be presenting some facts to him and maybe the kind of responses, so we would then know whether we could go down the path and how far down the path. We, I expect, will get a response on that, having the opportunity perhaps to speak to Mr. Kostic a little later. I'm not aware of how long he's going to be in The Hague on this particular visit, but clearly if he is here and he is available, we would be very happy to meet with him and discuss these issues, and maybe even follow one particular course which I understand others have found meaningful, which is to sit down and go through the indictment, as it were, word by word and see where we are ad idem and can agree facts or agree issues and where we cannot, which would then certainly help to streamline the evidence, I think. So that is the present position regarding that. We have not made progress in that sense in a practical way, I'm afraid, but we certainly -- as I say, I think the goodwill is there on both sides to do so, and we are very happy to accommodate Mr. Kostic whenever he's available. He, after all, is one man, and we are a greater number, so I'm sure we can make the effort to accommodate him more easily. Having said that, Your Honours, you've also referred to the other matters, a pre-trial brief being the first that is listed here. The very first draft of that has been completed and is in our hands, so we are now going to be working with that brief alongside the preparation of the evidence so that the two marry up together and hopefully produce the suitably meaningful document that you will be looking for. As to a list of witnesses, essentially that is a matter that we can prepare within the next two -- sorry. Am I going too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We will deal with this issue in somewhat greater detail later on. I should perhaps first hear the Defence concerning this first meeting that took place. Mr. Kostic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had a meeting after the last Status Conference. I think that was a positive meeting because I think that both Mr. Terrier and Mr. Blaxill and Ms. Chana and I discussed -- I think it was more of conceptually to discuss how perhaps we can accomplish this, and I think some progress was made. I also received a draft from them, albeit it was a short draft, of some ideas and facts which is helpful to me, and I think we can make some progress. I will be back next week and we can do that. The only thing that I think might have made it a little difficult from looking at the draft that they had is that when I looked at some of the suggestions, I did not discover the items in my discovery yet. In other words, I hadn't received those documents yet. So it's very difficult for me to make that determination without actually seeing the documents, but I think we'll keep trying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kostic. Mr. Blaxill, as regards the pre-trial brief, I think that during the last Status Conference I suggested that the pre-trial brief should be the result of previous negotiations between the parties. So, therefore, it will be submitted at the end of the pre-trial phase. I hope that I was clear enough. If you read the Rules, you see that we have to have the brief at that time. The way we read the Rules is that the pre-trial brief constitutes the results and the fruit of the negotiations and meetings between the parties and, therefore, it can be submitted at the end of the pre-trial phase. I think that in that respect, you will have certain comments to make, but let me propose the date of the 26th of October. That date is contained in our scheduling order. So today, 10th of July, was initially the date that was fixed for a pre-trial Status Conference. You probably remember that. There were several dates for Pre-Trial Conferences, and today this was supposed to be the end of the pre-trial phase, and it seems we are now only at the beginning of the pre-trial phase. I should like to hear you on this issue, Mr. Blaxill. So as regards to the submission of the pre-trial brief, how do you link it with the proposed date, that is, with the date of the 26th of October, which is supposed to mark the end of the pre-trial phase?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. President, the fact is that what we have at this present time is essentially, let us say, a sterile version in that issues of fact and law and so forth are basically there as a skeleton to which we can work, and the idea is indeed that from now forward, we can keep this document in mind as the sort of crucial document of the dossier and it will thus be amended and tailored, if I may use that expression, as we go along and in the light of any negotiations and results of agreements or disagreements that we register with our learned friend Mr. Kostic. So that indeed the 26th of October, hopefully that will indeed be the date when that brief will have been concluded as a result of the work we can undertake hopefully in this early part of the summer prior to and even during the court recess in August so that we could have all these issues firmly settled and prepared for. So it is not a document that it purports in any way to be ready now. It is our working tool for the future work that is scheduled to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, Mr. Blaxill has mentioned a skeleton of the pre-trial brief, which has to be submitted prior to the 26th of October. What do you think of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I certainly have no problem with the dates. I have no problem with Mr. Blaxill's methods, and I'm sure that a lot of work will go into it. I'm not on the Prosecution's side, of course, so I have to be careful how I comment on that pre-trial brief, but I do assume, Judge, that there are some very, very serious and complicated issues, and perhaps it's good that the work will go on until the 26th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The next item is the list of witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call, the list which is provided for in Rule 65 ter (E)(iv). During the Status Conference of the 11th of April, the Prosecutor indicated its intention to call 140 -- 180 witnesses. In the scheduling order, we ordered the Prosecutor to endeavour not to call more than two witnesses on the same fact. Furthermore, in accordance with the scheduling order of the 4th of July, that list of witnesses has to be submitted on the 26th of October at the latest. Let me explain things a little further. During the last Status Conference, we invited the Prosecutor to distinguish between important and less important witnesses. In other cases conducted before this Tribunal, we have cases of the Prosecutor calling several witnesses on one and the same facts, sometimes even up to 15. When the Prosecutor says that he can contact the Defence and analyse the indictments, I think that they should also try to find undisputed matters of law and fact while doing so. As regards any potential disagreement, of course we have a number of facts that need to be established. In relation to those facts, I invite the Prosecutor not to call more than two witnesses. It is quite possible for the Prosecution and for the Defence to have a list of witnesses who can be called later on if you don't think that two witnesses will not be enough to prove what you want to prove. You will always have a list of witnesses that can be called later on. We have to proceed in an efficient way. I don't know what the reaction of the Prosecutor will be to this suggestion of the Chamber, expressed by the Pre-Trial Judge in this case. We all know the existence of this restriction in our respective national systems. I also think that there is a kind of psychological effect involved in this problem. If you call five witnesses at the beginning to prove certain facts, then it is very difficult later on to cut down the number of witnesses. However, if you decide to call only two witnesses to testify on the same fact and if later on you realise that there is still need for a third witness, I think that this is easier for all of us to proceed in that manner. Can I please hear you on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will perhaps jump the order of the agenda and move on to item 8, that is, the issue of deposition and witnesses called pursuant to Rule 71 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In the case we are dealing with today, unlike another case in which I am appearing, which the Tribunal is familiar, we are in the position to prove a certain precise number of facts which are enumerated in the indictment, that is, the issue of snipers and the issue of shelling. Today, we envisage to call 180 witnesses indeed. However, it is evident that if the Defence, during the summer break, that is, until September, it is possible that there is an incident which is mentioned in the indictment, and it is possible that such an attack is not conducted against a specific target, and we will have definitely more than one witness to establish these facts. If the position of the Defence was different, if the Defence affirms that the shelling is not an act committed by the members of the Romanija Corps, we will call two or three more witnesses to prove what we want to prove, that is, that the said units were under the control of the accused. Secondly, we are now doing the selection of our witnesses. We have witnesses which can testify in accordance with Article 84 bis of the Rule, that is, by affidavit, then we have witnesses that have to be called before a full Chamber of this Tribunal, and also witnesses who will testify pursuant to Rule 71 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As regards witnesses -- as regards, I'm sorry, item number 7 of the agenda, that is the affidavits, there will be no special difficulties in this case to collect affidavits because we have witnesses who live in Sarajevo who do not feel threatened in any way, and I don't think that there are any reasons for these witnesses to be threatened. So they will provide their assistance, and we can count on the full co-operation of the relevant authorities in Sarajevo. So we will be in the position to collect these affidavits and provide them as corroboration of evidence given by other witnesses, those who will be called to testify before the Tribunal, before the Chamber sitting in full composition or before a presiding officer. So we are making a distinction between these witness. So some of the witnesses will be testifying in a direct manner against the accused. They will be the so-called fact witnesses. There will also be witnesses who will try to establish the responsibility of the accused in relation to those facts. I think that such witnesses will have to be called to testify before the Chamber so that the Chamber can be in a better position to establish the responsibility of the accused. So this concerns the procedure pursuant to Rule 71, and we suggest that this procedure be used by the Chamber. In our work, we are well aware of the concerns of the Tribunal, and we are trying to reduce the time of hearing which will be necessary for this case. So this is one of the main concerns of the Prosecution, and I am convinced that in that perspective, although this may not always be the case, that with Mr. Kostic we will have a most fruitful co-operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Terrier. Mr. Kostic, we're talking about Prosecution witnesses. Perhaps that is not the moment for you to comment, but you could perhaps tell us, how do you intend to prepare your defence? And regarding Rule 94 ter, the affidavit witnesses under the conditions mentioned by Mr. Terrier, and there is another point under item 8 of the agenda, that is, Rule 71. Mr. Terrier made a distinction about calling witnesses before the Trial Chamber of Judges and other witnesses who might be called to testify before Presiding Officers. What are your views on this, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I'm going to attempt not to conjecture too much, because I don't know what the strategy of the Prosecution is, other than very generally from the indictment. I can foresee, once witnesses are identified and we have an idea as to what they may wish to state to the Chamber, we may be able to do some depositions. It's a technique that we're very familiar with, and I generally don't have a problem with that, Your Honour. I'm a little more concerned about the affidavit form of testimony. That to me is a little more bothersome, but I think if the witnesses are identified, we can evaluate that procedure. My only concern on the deposition cases is I can tell you, and again I'm conjecturing, please excuse me because I haven't maybe fully thought it through, is the issue of the fact that of course, the accused has a right to be present at proceedings of the Chamber, and that is just one issue that concerns me. I think we can treat that as we get along in this case, but so you know ahead of time, that is just one of my concerns. Because as you know oftentimes, a deposition will take place at some other location and that, of course, creates logistical problems because General Galic is here and will be here unless you change that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, another point under point 2 is the list of exhibits which the Defence wishes to produce. I think mention is made of exhibits which the Defence must notify as to whether they contest their authenticity or not. Regarding that point, Mr. Blaxill, your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As regards the exhibits, at this point in time, a substantial number of documentary exhibits have already been identified and selected. A number of them do, in fact, attract at this time a Rule 70 provision and, therefore, we are making an application. Mostly it is a United Nations documentation. We don't understand there to be a problem over this or any resistance to the release from Rule 70. Simply we must comply with a request procedure which may take two or three weeks to result, and then they would be duly disclosed. The exhibits will be thus put together and listed. Therefore, I anticipate and we anticipate this will be done in short order during the summer and there will be plenty of time for consultation again with my friend Mr. Kostic so that we can see what can be agreed, whether the authenticity of documents can be agreed, and where indeed we may have a problem and need, say, to call a witness to prove them. That being said, I anticipate both with the list of witnesses and exhibits, these are documents which again are going to be kind of working documents up to the final date in October when, hopefully, some will be on or off that list depending on what we need to prove and in what ways we can save time at the end of the day for the actual trial. So I think that's all I propose to say in relation to the exhibits issue at this time, Your Honours. There is only one other point which kind of really is an overriding situation and applies to all matters of disclosure and in a sense preparation, and that is this, that particularly with regard to our Rule 68 obligation, we undertake a complete and detailed computer search of the data banks and the evidence banks of the Tribunal, Office of the Prosecutor. At this point in time, the computer evidence section have told us that they will be performing a search on 1.5 million documents. They use several -- tens if not hundreds of key words to multiply the approaches of the search in an endeavour to ensure, we hope, within the bounds of technology, every relevant reference that can be gained from the archives of the evidence unit. Now, the simple fact of that is that we were advised they hope to commence this in respect of three large trials, this being one of them, and to run this work from July with a projected conclusion date of November, the end of November. However, I understand there was a software delay and the task will begin in August. Now, the reality there is of course we are in the hands of what is going to be a large resource working very hard, flat out, to produce the documentation, to cross refer every reference and see that the evidence be fully checked in our archives. Now, that being said, of course, we cannot make promises that we cannot keep. Therefore, it may be that some documents will obviously emerge in the course of this, will need to be served, and things will need to be adjusted. I am, however, advised that we will be getting virtually a weekly submission of computer hits and documents. So what it really means is that we do not wait until November and then face some awesome task of checking documentation. We basically will have a weekly update. So that by the time this finishes, even if the process is going beyond our trial-ready date in October, it would be in respect of, I trust, a small amount of adjustment between them and the trial. I thought I should mention that. Of course there is the issue of any reciprocal disclosure that may be required by the Defence, where again searches would have to be run to assist and co-ordinate that. That is a matter which, in a sense, rests with my learned friend, Mr. Kostic, and what decisions he makes. But, of course, there may be some issues where we would wish to exercise any reciprocal rights in respect to documents in his possession. I hope, Your Honour, that covers any concerns you have regarding, as it were, the documentary preparation at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Blaxill. I would have at least three points to take up. You mentioned the list of exhibits, and we quite agree with you, that depends on what you intend to prove. But in relation to this list of exhibits, did you bear in mind a recommendation that we made before to prepare in advance a list of exhibits so that it should be ready for discussion, so as to save time here in the courtroom? I see Mr. Terrier saying yes but I should like to hear from you. I've seen, I haven't heard, your reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It is in the affirmative, Your Honours, yes. The whole purpose, I think, is that whatever we are preparing at this stage, we are doing it in the broadest terms so that we can work towards a streamlined product as we deal with our learned friend, Mr. Kostic. As the issues become clear, we can sweep some things off, put other things on, and then make sure that at the end, hopefully we have the efficient kind of documents that we're looking for in due time for the dates in October. That is the purpose. So the answer, sir, is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another point is that the Chamber really doesn't expect miracles from you. We know that the Prosecutor has many powers, but I still think that you are not endowed with the power of making miracles. So we're counting on your human abilities, and it is quite logical to say that as you go along, as you have at your disposal these documents, you will communicate them to Mr. Kostic, knowing that Mr. Kostic will probably be inclined to do exactly the same thing in a spirit of reciprocity. I now turn to Mr. Kostic to see whether he has any responses, comments, or suggestions to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think in this regard, Your Honour, I really don't have a comment. I think I've listened to Mr. Blaxill carefully, and he seems to be confident that he can do what he said he will try to do, and that's all I can -- I can agree with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another point. We have already spoken about affidavits, deposition testimony by Presiding Officers. The next point is the third on the agenda, that is, the possibility of reducing the number of issues in dispute through judicial notice, pursuant to Rule 94 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. If I may -- because, after all, it is up to the parties to construct their case -- I would like you to mention a few names to see, by association, what is your reaction. I'm referring, for instance, to Tadic, Celebici, and if we're talking about the Rule 61 hearings of Karadzic and Mladic. What would be your reactions? It's an extensive project, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours, and we do have the human frailties that you've rightly attributed to us. That is, in many ways, I think, along the lines that we have been thinking. We have not had the time or opportunity, really, to address it as a practical project to put together. But, yes, we were proposing, in essence, by using the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and the judgements of the cases to date, in a sense to go from appellate judgements, where we feel that they, by their very nature, are the highest judgements of the Tribunal, and therefore judicial notice or, indeed, adjudicated fact issues may well be put forward that way. Of course, then the various judgements in the cases Your Honours have referred to of completed trials where there are judgements at first instance, again to see where certain facts or issues can be at least suggested with some confidence as being something Your Honours may take judicial notice of, or again try and argue them to be adjudicated fact for the purposes of the given proceedings. Then finally, I suppose, to look with some care, obviously, at issues that are currently under appeal from certain opinions at first instance, because clearly it may be we may not have such confident ground to move forward if it is still disputed before the Appellate Chamber. But I'm certainly thinking along those very lines, Your Honours, that from the judgements of the very Tribunal, I think we have a primary source for hopefully getting some judicial notice issues to place before you. I think, then, our secondary approach may be even more an historical one, where hopefully certain issues relating to the Balkan conflict itself, certain sort of dates or times or places, things of common knowledge, as it were, from the public domain might also be added to that. So we basically take a jurisprudential basis from the Tribunal and add, perhaps, the popular understanding of the conflict to amplify those facts. That would be, I think, a way forward we would be looking to try and address the issue of judicial notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Mr. Kostic, one perhaps could go a little further already than mere conjecture. What are your ideas regarding these questions that have been raised and the ideas that Mr. Blaxill has just presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I'm normally a little reluctant to put facts into the judicial notice category, and I think that's probably just coming from the fact that I've been a defence attorney for many years and I think that makes me a little hesitant, because what it means is that if those facts are accepted, they would have occurred in another litigation in which I was not involved. So that's why I have this, maybe, bit of a reluctance. I do think that there may be some matters that could be considered, perhaps some historical matters, perhaps some -- if there's some very strong appellate opinions. One thing that does concern me is that this -- the theme or actually the indictment in this case, so far, I believe, as I've been following the work of the Tribunal, is the first time that this particular matter has been taken up by the -- by any Trial Chamber. In other words, events in this area at this time -- at the time alleged. So I'm not sure how that may or may not help us. Some of the cases you've mentioned, I think there are other cases involved and other cases have been tried, so there may be some connections between them. And then finally, the Rule 61 hearing concerning General Mladic and President Karadzic was a sort of a unique hearing where there was -- it was not really a litigation in a classical sense. There was no adversarial system. In other words, it was purely the Prosecutor presenting facts in order to obtain an international warrant. That's why I have some reluctance in regard to that particular hearing. I'm not saying that there may not have been good witnesses and legitimate witnesses, but again I'm always concerned that only one team, to use a football analogy, if one only one team is playing on the field, Judge. But I think that it's worth exploring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that even if we are not in, strictly speaking, the area of judicial notice, I think one could always grasp chances for discussing matters and coming to a possible agreement. I think we can talk about judicial notice in relation to cases that have been finally judged. In relation to the Mladic and Karadzic hearings, we can talk about the admission of documents coming from the other case without referring to it as judicial notice. So I think that we must bear in mind there is a strictly technical definition of judicial notice, but there is a whole series of other things that don't fit into that technical definition but which can be discussed and on which agreement can be reached. So I leave you with this suggestion and proposition on my part. Let us now go on to point 4 -- no. Yes. Point 4 of the agenda, that is to say, whether the Defence has sought disclosure pursuant to Rule 66(B) and 67(C) of the Rules of Procedure. We have touched upon the question, but what we need to do now is to see whether Defence has already requested such disclosure from the Prosecutor. Have you done that, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in regard to that issue, we've had a few conversations, and it is my understanding that we're going to try to co-operate on this issue. In other words, yes. So far, for example, I have received some items in a photocopy form with the agreement that eventually, if I want to see the actual tangible item, let's say a photo or something of that nature, that will be shown to me. Likewise, whatever tangible evidence I would collect, whether it's photos or anything of that nature, obviously I would offer that to the other side. I don't think that this is going to be much of a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as for the Prosecutor, since the request has not yet been made but it is about to be made, does the Prosecutor wish to resort to Rule 67(C), since the Rule envisages the possibility but does not oblige the Prosecutor to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, indeed, Your Honours, I think in that sense I would like to resort to an ancient expression of keeping one's powder dry. I'm as hopeful as my learned friend, Mr. Kostic, that by simple mutual co-operation such issues as seeing each other's documentation and disclosing information from one side to the other will be something which would probably trouble the Chamber and trouble the Rules as least possible. Clearly, if at any time there is a problem for either, there are remedies that we can come and litigate over such issues, and therefore perhaps we could reserve our position in respect of 67(C) Your Honour. But hopeful, as I say, that by communication and co-operation, hopefully we will resolve any issues of mutual disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Point 5 of the agenda, the possible intention of the accused or the Defence to raise one of the defences, pursuant to Rule 67(A)(ii) of the Rules. The Defence has indicated that it may offer the defence of alibi for certain parts of the period covered by the indictment. Have you anything to add regarding this point, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the easier answer in regard to number 5 on your agenda is obviously the 67(A)(ii)(b). That is a very clear, no. That is not a defence that will be used in this case. In regard to the alibi defence, I'm sort of reserving that, Your Honour, and I'll tell you why, mainly because the time period is lengthy in the indictment. I know you're familiar with it, of course. And because I haven't quite seen every bit of discovery, I just want to reserve it in the event, for example, that some witness statement comes in a month or two down the road and says General Galic was at such-and-such location on such-and-such date, and if, in fact, he wasn't, and I want to present that evidence, which is alibi evidence, I would like to be able to reserve that. Generally though, generally, and so far I have not seen anything in the discovery I have received so far which would cause me to tell you that we would use the alibi defence. But I consider this a continuing duty, Judge, to let you know if something like this occurs, and if something like this occurs, I would immediately file a notice in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, I think it should be noted that if General Galic was somewhere else on a particular date, it is not a witness that is going to come and say so. General Galic knows that well. There's a second remark I wish to make, and that is that you must communicate, according to Rule 67, to the Prosecutor -- you must notify the Prosecutor of this and, in any event, prior to the commencement of the trial. I wish this to be noted in the transcript. You must do so prior to the commencement of the trial. And as you know, the Prosecutor, if you notify him of this, then the Prosecutor has a reciprocal communication to make in response. I think this is something that has to be clear. The defence of alibi is not going to crop up today but something that has already occurred. I think you have to bear this in mind. I know you're doing that, but this is just to remind you. We're now going to pass on to item 6 of the agenda, and that is the possible intention of the accused to testify or to make a statement under Rule 84 bis of the Rules, and if so, at what stage of the proceedings. Mr. Kostic, on the basis of the documents analysed and your discussions with the Prosecution, have these helped you to take a decision in that respect? This Status Conference is simply to make a checklist of all the questions that we have to address and prepare for. So I am now asking you the question, Mr. Kostic. Do you have a definite idea about this already or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the basis of the discovery that I have obtained and reviewed, I would say that General Galic would testify during the Defence's case in chief, not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you can answer a following question. He will testify at the beginning of the examination-in-chief -- Defence case-in-chief or at the end of Defence case-in-chief? I have just been reminded by the interpreter. Mr. Kostic has indicated that his client would testify during the Defence's case-in-chief. If possible, could you tell us, at this point, is that going to take place at the beginning of your case, in the middle of your case, or the end of your case? Could you tell us that now, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think there are an awful lot of factors that go into making that decision. Part of it has to do with the state of the Prosecutor's case by the time he finishes. General Galic, as you know, as to his own testimony has a right -- in fact, he has a right not to testify, I assume, but he will make that decision also. I will help him with that decision. It may be premature to tell you that. I'm not trying to be cute, as we say in the United States, in other words, to evade your question. I may not be able to answer it. I can tell you that typically I would envision that the testimony would occur later in the presentation of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you that we already have a practice at this Tribunal that the accused have already testified at the beginning of the trial, even before the Prosecution case, but I'm sure you're familiar with that fact. When the accused testify at the end of the Defence case, there are far too many repetitions, and we often have the impression that if the accused had testified at the beginning of the Prosecution case, many witnesses would not have had to come to testify. But as you have indicated, Mr. Kostic, General Galic is going to make a decision for himself on this issue. So we have dealt with issues 7 and 8 already, that is, the collection of affidavits and formal statements and depositions as well. We should perhaps limit ourselves to what we have said about the matter and move on to item number 9, which is the schedule. The first Status Conference -- during the first Status Conference on the 11th of April, we tried to establish a schedule together. In view of the situation today, I think that it is necessary to make certain changes in respect to that schedule. I have to remind you that the pre-trial phase is also a working period like the trial itself. We consider the pre-trial phase at this Chamber as a working stage of the procedure as a whole, just like the trial itself. As regards the preparation, if we want to have a good quality preparation, we have to fix realistic deadlines, realistic time limits. As things stand now, we have two status conferences scheduled for the 6th and the 12th of October. Another one is scheduled for the 18th of October, 2000, and the idea is that the parties inform us about the progress that has been made in respect of the preparation of the case and to ensure that they are able to work together. We have to sort of oblige you to work together in parallel so that you can have an opportunity to get together and organise yourselves. These conferences will enable the parties to tell us about their pre-trial briefs and the situation with their pre-trial briefs, and they will also be able to tell us how they stand concerning the provisions of Rule 65 ter (E). The deadline for the submission for the Prosecution has been fixed for the 26th of October, 2000. The Defence has to submit its pre-trial brief, provided for under Rule 65 ter (E), (F), the 10th of November at the latest, and a Pre-Trial Conference provided for in Rule 73 is scheduled for the 22nd of November, 2000 because it was not possible for that Status Conference to take place today. We have already discussed the submission of pre-trial briefs in accordance with Rule 65 ter (E), and now I should like to hear the Defence concerning the submission of its pre-trial brief in view of the date that I have indicated, that is, the 10th of November, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: In looking at what needs to be done from today into October 26th and then the date of the 10th of November, I believe, Judge, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have four months, Mr. Kostic. Sorry to interrupt you, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I do -- in order to respond, I do need to see the final product from the Prosecutor, which is filed on the 26th, and I think it would be helpful to me, and I think it would make it maybe a more even situation if I did get some additional time. I think it's a little tight, the 14 days that you are allowing us here. I think it's a bit too short for us to do all of the things we need to do between the 26th and the 10th, and I would ask the Court's indulgence to grant us some additional time. I'm just afraid that that's a very short period of time, and I think it would perhaps even improve our submissions if we had some additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I had in mind as regards Status Conferences, was that we at least have certain time limits. You know that the time factor is very important when this comes to the organisation of our work. As I told you already, today's date was initially scheduled for a Pre-Trial Conference, and I don't think that we can accept the idea that Pre-Trial Conferences are something that we are going to have from time to time. Status Conferences need to be properly organised and Pre-Trial Conference is the last one in line. As I already told you, if there are very good reasons, exceptional reasons indeed, we can deviate from the schedule. We are not the slaves of the organisation, of course. It is the organisation of the work that has to serve our purpose. But be that as it may, I think that in order to obliged all of us to work hard, it is very good to have a schedule even if it's only a provisional one. Mr. Fourmy has drawn my attention to something that I have forgotten in the agenda, and, I'm sorry, we have to go back to number 9, that is, schedule for the submission of reports by expert witnesses pursuant to Rule 94 bis. Do you have anything to say on this matter at the moment? Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours. We anticipate at this time that six expert witnesses will be necessary for the purposes of the Prosecution case. Essentially they will be of carrying forms of military expertise in the main. I can say that in respect of -- I believe, from memory, three if not four persons have already been served as part of the 66(A)(ii) material, so obviously, we would have to reserve them under the approach Rule to be agreed or not agreed as the Rule provides. But to that extent at least, my learned friend would have had good advanced warning of the contents of their potential evidence, which will doubtless be amplified and tailored into appropriate form for giving their evidence as experts during the trial. Again, that's a matter, we trust, that in the course of this summer will be finalised and open for comment and debate with my learned friend Mr. Kostic, and we'll see where we can go from there in terms of saving court time if they can be accepted as in writing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blaxill, do you have any idea of the number of pages and the size of these documents, expert witness reports? If you do not, just tell us so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't know as such. But from certain of the draft work I have seen so far or have been involved in, you are not looking at massive volumes. I would not anticipate any of them presenting to Your Honours 100 or 200 pages worth of expertise. These will be focused, we trust, and will be concise documents. Not volumes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I was going to give Mr. Kostic the opportunity to respond, but actually I would like to hear him on a different matter. When we have this type of document, that is, very voluminous documents, in another case we agreed that the translation should be made only of the conclusions contained therein, because you are familiar with the problem of translation at this institution. So at least in that way, the accused will have the opportunity to read the conclusions in his language. However, if we want to translate the whole document, this will take us a large amount of time. So I should like to hear Mr. Kostic in respect of what the Prosecutor has just stated, and also I should like to hear his view of what I have just suggested, that is, the proposal that the Prosecutor provides the translation only of the conclusions contained in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have received what I believe are either two or three expert opinions. They were not identified as such because they were disclosed under a different Rule. But looking at some of that, I think that I'm still -- I'm reviewing that, and the issue is going to be if there needs to be hired an expert who is going to counter the findings or the conclusions and the opinion of the expert, then that could be an issue. What I'm saying to you is if, for example, the expert report is only in B/C/S and the potential expert doesn't understand, then that's problematic and, of course, vice versa. So that's the only problem that I would have. What I'm going to try to do is to identify a potential Defence witness on the various topics -- as I say, I've got two or three -- and if there is an issue in that regard, I will deal with Mr. Blaxill, see if we can work something out. Obviously, as you know, if we can't resolve our issues, we're going to come to you and let you resolve it. But I will try to do that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have covered the entire agenda now. It was like a checklist of all the items that need to be considered, discussed, and prepared so that we can reach the end of the pre-trial stage and so that we can begin the trial in an appropriate manner. We have already stated the schedule for our Status Conferences. By that time we will know the results of your co-operation. In the meantime we can also give you some guidelines for our following Status Conferences as well. We have been working for an hour and a quarter and we still have to deal with the motion for provisional release submitted by General Galic. I think it is better for us to continue without making a break; otherwise we risk running out of time. As regards the motion for provisional release by the Defence in this case, a motion hearing in respect of that motion will also enable us to review the defence of the accused. Let us now remind ourselves of the procedural background. The motion for provisional release, dated the 7th of April, 2000, was filed on the 13th of April, 2000. On the 11th of May, 2000, the Chamber issued a ruling scheduling a hearing on the 18th of May, 2000, the subject of the hearing being the Defence motion for provisional release. The Defence has requested that a hearing on that motion be postponed because it had planned to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina to gather appropriate evidence and to secure certain guarantees and commitments from the relevant authorities of the government of Republika Srpska concerning the provisional release of the accused. The Chamber therefore postponed the motion hearing on the 8th of June, 2000. General Galic was present at the hearing, and Mr. Kostic told us that the relevant decision was not transmitted to his office. The Registrar has indicated to the Chamber that knowing that Mr. Kostic was in The Hague between the 23rd and the 25th of May, 2000, its office sent a letter to his office in accordance with the usual procedure. The mailbox, however, was never emptied. At the hearing of the 8th of June, Mr. Kostic was not in a position to argue his motion for provisional release. The Chamber therefore gave an additional 15 days, that is, until the 23rd of June, 2000, for the filing of the necessary documents in support of the motion. The Chamber also gave an opportunity to the Prosecutor to respond to the motion. The documents were filed on the 23rd of June, 2000 and they consist of a declaration made by Mr. Kostic, a statement signed by the accused, General Galic, and a statement signed by his wife. There has been a reply to the Prosecutor's response and also a letter addressed to Republika Srpska, dated 20 June 2000. In this letter, certain guarantees in respect of provisional release were requested. The Prosecutor responded on the 29th of June, but no guarantees have come from the authorities of Republika Srpska to this date. Mr. Kostic, since he was not able to argue his motion on the scheduled date because he had not been informed of the postponement for the 23rd of June, he -- it was the result of his lack of due diligence. In view of the decisions made by the Chamber, certain guarantees have been provided, but further guarantees are necessary in support of the motion. However, to this date they have not been provided. Instead, Mr. Kostic has simply filed a letter which was addressed to the government of Republika Srpska, which letter is dated only the 20th of June, 2000. In view of his conduct concerning this issue, it seems that the Defence has not shown due diligence, and in accordance with Article 6 of the Code of Conduct for Defence counsel appearing before the International Tribunal, in accordance with the provisions of that Article, the Defence counsel are requested to comply with Article 44(B), and also in accordance with the relevant provisions of the said Code. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber wishes to remind you that it has already noted its deep concern as regards the fact that Mr. Kostic submitted, on behalf of the Defence, a preliminary motion which was clearly not based on the criminal procedure which is applicable before this Tribunal. The Trial Chamber finds itself, therefore, obliged to declare that every new motion by the Defence which will not be in compliance with the general Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal will be considered as a serious failure to comply with the obligations of the Defence. Other preliminary motions were also rejected by the Trial Chamber, the preliminary motions that were filed on the same day. One of the motions disputed the form of the indictment. Such a motion was submitted after the expiration of the time limits provided for in Rule 72 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The submission of this motion has once again illustrated the failure of the Defence counsel to comply with the relevant provisions of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In accordance with Article 20(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal, the Chamber must ensure that the accused has a fair trial and due process and that the procedure is being conducted in accordance with such provisions. This requirement is of a particular importance in view of the seriousness and the gravity of the charges against the accused and the punishment that can be imposed if he is found guilty. One of the principal rights of the accused is contained in Article 21(4) of the Statute. In accordance with that provision, each time that the interests of justice requires so, the accused must be assigned a defence counsel. This provision is based on the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and it is repeated in the European and the American Convention on Human Rights. In accordance with the jurisprudence of the Committee for Human Rights, and also in accordance with the jurisprudence of the European Court for Human Rights and the American Court for Human Rights, this right guarantees to the accused an efficient defence. In the Code of Conduct and the directive concerning the assignment of counsel before the Tribunal, this requirement is also reflected. Although the conduct of the Defence is an issue which has to be debated between counsel and his client, the Trial Chamber is required to intervene if it appears that the accused may be denied an efficient defence. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber, considering the concern which it has expressed on several occasions and also aware of its statutory obligations, wishes to make a note that will be made part of the record that it has formally warned, cautioned, Mr. Kostic, who has been assigned to the accused, of this issue, and it has cautioned him that conduct which is contrary to the relevant provisions may entail action pursuant to Rule 46 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. You have heard what the Trial Chamber has had to note and, Mr. Kostic, I have to say that what the Trial Chamber wanted to do was to share publicly its concerns. It is not a final condemnation, if I may say so. We just wish to remind you that we have to make an effort to make up for lost time. Now we have to go into the merits of the motion for provisional release of General Galic. We will begin with the Defence, who is the moving party in this issue, and after that I will leave the floor to the Prosecutor. Mr. Kostic, let us hear you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the submission which we made and which you have in front of you consists of statements of General Galic, of his wife. There is also a reply to the Prosecutor's response, which is more of a legal document arguing legal principles, and a letter from the Defence counsel to Republika Srpska. I have indicated to the Court, in paragraph 2, that I drafted the statements for the General and his wife in consultation with them, taking statements from them and actually translating as I spoke to them from Serbian into English when composing the statements. I did that in order that maybe we would shortcut some of the potential hearings, because if General Galic and his wife were called to testify, they would tell the Chamber pretty much what is in those two statements, and I don't think that we've left anything out. So that was the purpose of those two statements which are paragraph 2 of my statement. As I said, the reply to the Prosecutor is something that we have filed. I think that we don't need to argue beyond that, only in a short form. I have also indicated to the Tribunal that I've had a number of meetings with the various individuals who are in the Government of Republika Srpska, and have learned from them the progress in regard to the co-operation between the government of Mr. Dodik and the Tribunal, his visits to the Tribunal, and his concern for what is going on here, also the fact that he has appointed Mr. Jovicic, who is a former judge, as I indicated in my statement, who is the liaison officer. Now, in paragraph 6 of my statement, I indicate that I had a number of conversations with Mr. Jovicic, who has indicated, and I quote from him, that the Government of Republika Srpska is prepared to send any appropriate letters and documents to the Trial Chamber, if it so orders, which would guarantee the appearance of General Galic at all Court hearings, that they would supervise any release and ensure that any court ordered obligations be performed by General Galic. In discussing the matter of a potential provisional release, Mr. Jovicic has indicated that essentially what has occurred, at least in, I believe, one or two prior cases which are cited in my brief, the Simic case and the other matter, and that was that essentially what occurred is that once the Court has agreed that it would grant the motion for provisional release, before the Court would do that, they would want Mr. Jovicic to be present in The Hague, to bring the letters, to bring aeroplane tickets, to do all of the information that is necessary. In other words, Mr. Jovicic would then become an integral part in the process. And the way I described the process to me, I would then, if asked by the Chamber, I would be prepared to come and discuss the issues dealing with the release and the obligations. For that reason is why my discussions with Mr. Jovicic occurred in May, sometime between, I would believe, the 12th and the 26th of May, and it was his instructions that I needed a letter as a -- the type of letter which I've attached to my submission, and that I would then, if the Court ruled so, I would then, of course, attend a hearing here if the Court felt that it was willing to grant provisional release with the obligations that the Government of Republika Srpska would honour, would follow, and would guarantee, and I asked that that come -- that that directive be from a Trial Chamber. But he's prepared to do that. I have indicated that in my statement, and I wouldn't have done that unless Mr. Jovicic has indicated to me that they are prepared to do that. The only other information that I think the Court should consider is the fact that in the response by the Prosecution, there was a matter introduced which dealt with a letter by General Galic and the nature of that letter. I had touched upon or I think the Defence has touched upon the letter in General Galic's statement. This has to do with the fact that at one point, General Galic had indicated that he was looking for some housing because he was in the process of losing his. What I would like to do, Your Honour, with the Court's indulgence, and I think that General Galic is prepared to do that, I think he's prepared to testify as to that particular issue if you would allow him to do that. I would not have much else to add to my submission, because I think it's fairly complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Kostic. As you know, the accused here speak through their attorneys. We are not yet at trial for General Galic to take his oath and testify. It's up to you to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: He's prepared to testify on that issue, Your Honour, the issue as to his situation at one point concerning the letters which are attached to the Prosecutor's submission. I can certainly make an offer of proof which might satisfy you, which would shortcut and curtail the General's testimony, and I'm certainly prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Only in regard --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: If you wanted me to make an offer of proof as to what General Galic would testify to in regard to that particular letter, I would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may explain what is the meaning of the letter. It is not a question of making an offer of proof or opening a trial on that issue. You can tell us what the meaning of the letter is. You have spoken about it with General Galic, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know from the statement that was filed on behalf of General Galic, which was composed on the basis of his statement, I had indicated that through his military service and the way the war developed in the former Yugoslavia, I had lost his home in Slovenia where he was assigned and where he was on duty as a JNA officer before the war broke out. Then I moved on to -- he was ordered by the JNA to move to the territory of Bosnia, and I remained there and was not allowed -- when the JNA was withdrawn from Bosnia to Serbia, the orders were such that officers and soldiers who were not -- who were born in Bosnia were to remain there, not relocate to Serbia. So at that time, I stayed in Bosnia and served in the Bosnian Serb army. Because I had no home, I lost in Slovenia, he was able to obtain a home sometime during the war. Unfortunately, as he has indicated, that particular apartment belonged to somebody else. It was vacated by a person who had fled from Banja Luka at some point during the war, and General Galic was assigned that particular apartment. As time progressed and after the war, the signing of the Dayton peace agreement and all the issues had begun to be resolved in regard to the refugee returns, there were a number of regulations, a number of Statutes throughout Bosnia, both in one and the other entity, which dealt with the return of homes and apartments. During that process, General Galic -- this was sometime now in early 1999, late 1998 -- was informed that the home which he was occupying had to be vacated because the prior owner had an interest of returning or claiming it or whatever, but issue was that he had to relocate. So that was one issue which caused him to think about whether or not he could reside in that home or had to vacate. The other issue had to do with the fact that I and his wife, as I've indicated in my submission, in the statement which was submitted by both the General and his wife, was the fact that they're taking care of an 81-year-old mother who is very ill, who is literally an invalid and cannot move. She is a pensioner in Serbia or in Yugoslavia, and, therefore, if she remains in Banja Luka in Bosnia where she was living with General Galic and his wife and had continued, she was not allowed to have any kind of social benefits, which of course, for somebody who is elderly, that includes medical care, and the state or Republika Srpska would not cover any of her medical benefits. So she did not gain those. They had to take care of all of that. So that was another issue, and that had to do with the fact that they felt that if perhaps if they could get an apartment in Serbia, she would be covered. That's another reason. Finally, I think that he was also concerned about the fact that some of the arrests which he was aware of included a certain amount of violence through the years. There was an individual who was killed in Prijedor during the arrest, there was -- there were other kinds of arrests, breaking down the doors and all those kinds of things, and those were very problematic, and the General really felt that I did not wish to have his family there to perhaps witness that or be involved in that or in any way be affected by that. Those, essentially, were the three motivations in seeking some alternate housing. The General himself wanted to and did remain in Banja Luka. As I've indicated to you, that's where his ancestral home is, that's where he has his brothers and sisters, that's where his job was, that's where I worked, and, quite frankly, even at the time of the arrest, he had followed a particular route and a routine, and, fortunately was arrested outside the home. The General has indicated in his submission that I would personally guarantee, regardless of the guarantees by the Government of Republika Srpska, that I would guarantee that I would abide by any of the conditions of a release that the Court would find would be appropriate. Certainly the kinds of obligations and guarantees that are in the letter which I have submitted is something that I would honour. And then finally, I think he's someone who, I think, is a respected military officer for many, many years, and I think he's somebody who, when I swears an oath that he will do something, I does that, and I think in this case I do not see him as an individual who would in any way shirk any of the obligations that I would have under any provisional release order or, or would there be anything to fear from him in regard to any witnesses or victims in this situation. In fact, I find it somewhat -- I would find it very, very difficult to imagine that I would, for example, leave Republika Srpska and go to the Federation and go to Sarajevo where -- I think, essentially almost every witness in this case lives in and around that area. I think if -- he could live with the conditions and -- that were provided in the other cases. So those, I think, are the -- if he was to -- if I would have testified, Your Honour, that is the type of testimony that I would have given you this afternoon; in other words, his motivations as to why I sought that particular apartment. Incidentally, there is a response that is attached to the Prosecutor's response, a response from the authorities in Serbia, which pretty much refuse him any kind of comfort or any kind of home or any kind of an apartment even though he is a career JNA individual who has retired. He has not appealed that decision that was tendered to him by that letter, and I think, if anything, the refusal to even offer him some housing in Serbia has more than cemented his own idea that I really does belong in Banja Luka, he made the right decision to go there initially in 1991, to stay there, to retire there, and to remain living there, and that's where I belongs and that's where I wants to go back. So that is essentially, Judge, what the General would testify to, and I hope that -- I'm not sure if I've done it as well I could have if I would have testified, but I'm trying to give the Court as much as I think I would testify if he could take the stand. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kostic. The Prosecutor. Do you wish to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Ms. Sureta Chana. Am I pronouncing your name correctly? Here we learn a lot of languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If it pleases the Chamber, I will address the issue of provisional release. Excuse me while I ... Your Honours, the Prosecutor opposes the motion for provisional release filed by the accused. I refer the Chamber to our written submissions filed on 20th April and the Prosecutor's further response dated 29th June, and now incorporate the same into my oral submissions on the motion for provisional release before this Chamber. Your Honours, Rule 65 enjoins the Defence to demonstrate to this Chamber and to the satisfaction of the Chamber of two conditions which must be met before this Chamber can grant provisional release. Firstly, Your Honours, it is that the accused will appear for trial if released; and secondly, that the accused will not pose a danger to any victim or witnesses or any other person. The Rule also stipulates, Your Honour, that the host country be heard to ascertain their position on this application for provisional release. To that end, Your Honours, on the 14th of April, 2000, the registrar did write to the government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and invited the Kingdom of Netherlands to submit its views and writings. Should no response be available, the Tribunal will proceed with its division under the presumption that the Kingdom of the Netherlands hold the opinion stated in a letter addressed to the registrar of the Tribunal dated the 18th of July, 1996. In this letter of 1996, the government of the Netherlands makes it quite clear that it does not wish to concern itself on the merits of provisional release but confines itself purely to the practical consequences of such a release, which basically entails the Visa or the permits that the accused might need to readmit himself to Holland or leave the territory, because as soon as he leaves the Scheveningen detention centre, he is no longer in the hands of the Tribunal. The accused, of his own initiative, has failed to ascertain the position of the host country as to whether he'll be readmitted into the Netherlands if released. The onus in this regard, Your Honours, does rest with the accused. So the position of the host country, I think we can take it, is in the negative. The burden of proof to satisfy the Chamber for the accused's provisional release rests squarely on the shoulders of the Defence. It is the Prosecutor's respectful submission that the accused has failed to discharge this burden to the satisfaction of the Chamber. The Defence has attempted to discharge this burden of proof by its own statement to the Chamber: a statement of the accused, a statement by the accused's wife, and, thirdly, a letter written by learned counsel for Mr. Jovicic of Republika Srpska in an attempt to secure and guarantee from Republika Srpska to ensure that the accused will be handed back to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to stand trial. Your Honour, my learned friend, in his oral submissions, attempted to explain why such a guarantee has not been forthcoming because he felt that this liaison officer has to be invited by this Chamber to issue such a guarantee. With respect, I disagree. If Mr. Jovicic was so minded to give this guarantee to the accused -- after all Mr. Kostic, by letter, had asked for one -- he would have been in a position to give one. Your Honour, if you look at the letter, I think it's interesting to note where the accused says, and I quote, and I think it bears quoting because it's very curious: "I am on the list of accused for the so-called war crimes during the war in BH from 1991 to 1995. For this reason," and I emphasise here, "and at the suggestion of the President of Republika Srpska and the person in charge of Republika Srpska, it has been suggested to me that I move out of the territory." The point here being, Your Honours, that any guarantee which might be forthcoming from Republika Srpska can hardly be taken seriously in light of the fact that it was the President himself who invited the accused to leave the territory. Therefore, it is the respectful submission of the Prosecutor that the documents and the submissions tendered by learned counsel for the Defence are not enough to satisfy this Chamber that the accused will appear for trial or that he will not interfere with witnesses if granted provisional release. On the contrary. The Prosecutor has tendered proof by a letter, the letter that I just quoted, emphasising his need for protection from the so-called war crimes Tribunal. Mr. Kostic, in his oral submissions to the Chamber this afternoon, has said there were three motivations which propelled the accused to write such a letter: One is relocation, simply because he'd lost his house in Slovenia; second was his aged mother so that she could get social benefits in Serbia; and thirdly was his fear of the violence which he might be subjected to while arrested. With due respect to Mr. Kostic, the letter actually says quite the contrary. Learned counsel has also made the submission that the accused is unlikely to venture into Federation territory to initiate acts of violence and intimidation. With respect to learned counsel, this is a very simplistic argument as acts of intimidation and violence do not necessarily require the accused to personally venture into Federation territory to initiate the same. We must also be mindful at this juncture that the accused has now been given names during disclosure of most of our witnesses who will testify at the Tribunal and, therefore, the likelihood of intimidation is increased now. Learned counsel also goes on to assert in his written submissions that "the Defence has received little documentation," and I quote, "from the Office of the Prosecutor." This again, with respect, is not an accurate representation of fact. The truth of the matter is that the Prosecutor has disclosed a sizeable amount of the case to the Defence. Your Honours, taking into account that the accused has been charged with the gravest offences under international humanitarian law, and also considering that if convicted the crimes will attract a long prison sentence, the incentive for the accused not to appear for trial by far outweighs that the accused will appear for trial if released. Once again, I go back to that letter which shows the true intent of the accused. It is now established jurisprudence, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber must make its determination as to provisional release in light of the particular circumstances of each case. It is our respectful submission, therefore, that the accused in this case has not fulfilled any of the conditions imposed upon him under Rule 65(B) and has not demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Chamber the existence of any circumstances which will justify his release by this Chamber. Therefore, we ask this Court not to grant provisional release to the accused, as to do so would be an extremely risky undertaking as the Tribunal, as we are aware, has no enforcement powers to ensure the return of the accused to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Your Honours, unless there is something else you wish me to address you upon, these are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, I just have one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Many of the factors that you listed as militating against the release of General Galic were also, of course, present in another Chamber's decision in the Tadic and Simic case, when the host country's position was the fact that Republika Srpska had not, in the past, had a long, admirable record of cooperating with the Tribunal. In those cases, apparently, at least that Chamber still granted release. What, if any factors, do you think are peculiar to this case that would distinguish this case from those? Obviously those are Trial Chamber holdings, although the Appeals Chamber refused to take an appeal from them. What do you think is different or special about this case so that this case would require a different result?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe in the other cases that you are referring to, this is something which we have incorporated at length in our response, is that the accused in one of those cases voluntarily surrendered and the time of trial, the detention, the period of incarceration before trial had become too lengthy. In our case, the accused has only been incarcerated for about six months, and there is no reason to believe that the trial is going to take a very long time. Even if you look at the European Convention On Human Rights, even up to two to three years is considered, for these kind of charges, to be quite reasonable under the circumstances. I think the distinguishing factor would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kostic, do you have any remarks or responses to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that a couple of things we should not forget. One is that the Tribunal began its work in 1994 -- 1993/1994 and continued on, and if there's one country in Europe which talks about the work of the Tribunal, it's Bosnia. In other words, all of the activities are covered. The General lived in one entity there for a number of years, for the last eight or nine years until his arrest. And I think what's significant is that he lived openly. He lived in a certain amount of public light. This was not some individual who was hiding in Prijedor or in Foca or someplace else. He was in the capital of the entity, he was, as my affidavit indicates, he was involved in government work, and he did not disappear into the background. Even after the arrests intensified, he continued living quite openly and not hiding and not running at that point. Even when he was refused the apartment, he continued living in Banja Luka openly and not hiding. I think that is an important factor to consider in this case. This was a sealed indictment case. This was not a warrant that sat some place and everybody knew about it and the person hid. He was, of course, unaware of its existence, but he also didn't do anything in any way to avoid if there was a service of that warrant. So I think that's one thing that I think is important in this particular case. I do think that each case has to be taken on its own merits, and I agree with my learned friend in that regard. I also think that maybe I disagree with my learned friend's, I think, commentary on the direction that Republika Srpska is taking in its co-operation and its relationship with the Tribunal. I think that they have turned a corner. I think they are involved, and again the visits to the Tribunal not only by the President but also by the Vice-President, the assigning of the office, the opening up of the office. Also I may add that it appears that in regard to the releases done by the other Chamber have been a success so far. Those individuals have honoured the obligations and have reported and done everything that's asked of them in that regard, and I think that's important to consider. In other words, Republika Srpska is doing its part to honour its obligations and its guarantees, and it's willing to do that in this particular case also. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kostic. The Chamber is going to consider all the arguments and the submissions that we have, and it will make a judgement in writing and not orally. A decision will be issued in writing as it is, indeed, an important decision. As I think all we have to do before adjourning is to give the floor to General Galic. General Galic, will you please stand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and tell the Chamber your observations regarding three points: the caution addressed to your counsel; secondly, your state of health; and three, conditions of detention. General Galic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can interrupt, I think it's improper, and I think it's an invasion of client-attorney privilege for General Galic to comment on point 1. I think it's very inappropriate for him to do that, and I think it's an invasion of the client-attorney privilege in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to accept your objection, Mr. Kostic. I wanted it to be written in the transcript that the Chamber was quite clear regarding this point. But I will grant you that it is a client-counsel privilege. I will ask General Galic to comment on his state of health and detention conditions. General Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first place, I would like to say good afternoon to Your Honours and to thank you for finding the time to hear me at such a late hour regarding my state of health. I can tell you, as I did last time, that nothing in particular has taken place. They're taking good care of me. Nobody has hurt me or offended me. I said last time, I hope that in year's time my condition regarding my injury will be improved. As for the rest of my health, it's quite good, but it would be welcome if we could reach a specialist more quickly. The whole procedure takes a long time. Regarding other detention conditions, there have been no significant changes since the last Status Conference and the conditions are quite acceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, General Galic, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to conclude, the Chamber is going to render its decision in writing regarding the motion of the Defence for provisional release. Regarding the Status Conference, we're going to wait for the next scheduled date to make an overview of the situation regarding developments, and I do encourage you to work hard because there is a lot to be done, and one has to be ready to work. I wish you success in your work until our next meeting. The meeting is adjourned.
